align.prompt: Run the LLM straighten ablation baseline for as-twn-taipei on the orig-llm-working2grid-haiku45 flow (forced re-run from scratch), then chain into the LLM network loop.

transcript.note: Round 1 — build shared lines rather than fix segments one at a time. The working2grid source is a near-random scatter (hv 6/74), so instead of nudging individual off-segments I picked a small set of anchor rows/cols and pulled whole chains onto them, always checking that the 360-degree bearing order at every degree>=3 endpoint is preserved. Anchors: row 3 (8-47-4, west tail), row 31 (36-44-40-17, the central east-west trunk), col 52 (34-17-30-31, the east trunk; 22 deliberately kept off col 52 so it does not land collinear-south of 17 behind 34 and swallow it), row 23 (23-12-22-46, the mid-east trunk), col 45 (40-10-9), col 39 (24-25-26), col 18 (45-33-15), row 41 (7-11-15; 7 slides along its own locked col 0 so the two existing V segments survive), row 0/col 42/col 29 for the small tails. Diagonals are preserved where a one-cell companion move keeps |dx|=|dy| (58 follows 36 to keep 36-58 at 45; 3 follows 2 to keep 2-3 at 45); 4-35 is upgraded to 45 since H/V is out of short range. Only 38-23 loses its diagonal, paid for by three new H/V around 23. Every move is within +/-3 cells and all 35 target cells are distinct and unoccupied.

Round 2 — two principles. (a) Upgrade 45-degree segments to H/V wherever one cell does it, since HV is the primary key: 6-13 becomes V on col 49 (13 slides one east and keeps 13-2 on row 7), 27-19 becomes H on row 52, 57-56 becomes V on col 7, 17-34 becomes H on row 31. (b) Extend the trunks built in round 1 rather than start new ones: 34 goes to (58,31) so it lands on the row-31 trunk AND on col 58 under 55, giving two segments from one move; 58 goes to (35,35) to sit under 44 on col 35 and west of 24 on row 35, likewise two; 22 slides east onto col 52 (its row-23 pair 12-22-46 survives because it stays on row 23) and 53 then drops onto the same col 52 while keeping 54-53 on row 14, so col 52 becomes 53-22-17-30-31. 18 and 37 move together three cells west so the existing 18-37 V is carried over intact while 18-20 becomes V on col 26. I verified no vertex ends up interior to any new straight segment (this is why 50 is NOT pushed onto row 58 — segment 49-50 would swallow 52 — and why 16 goes to row 41 rather than row 42, which is being reserved for 42-39). 35 and 42 are deliberate two-round moves: each is more than 3 cells from its target line, so this round covers part of the distance.

Round 3 — the easy H/V is gone (51/74), so this round splits into three kinds of move. (i) Real H/V still available: 35 completes its two-round walk onto col 9 under 4, and 42 completes its walk onto row 42 west of 39. (ii) A coupled pair to unlock 26-27: pushing 26 down onto row 52 would make segment 27-26 swallow 19, so 19 is simultaneously rotated from east of 27 to north of 27 — it stays aligned (H becomes V on col 27), row 52 is cleared, and 26-27 becomes H. I checked the circular order at 27 is the same cycle before and after. (iii) Where H/V is provably out of reach because both endpoints are already locked on a row and a col, I take the 45-degree upgrade instead, since HVD is the secondary key and these cost one cell each: 36-58, 38-23 (38 slides along its own locked col 42), 20-0 and 33-43 (both free leaf ends), plus 35-45 falls out of (i) for free. 40-12, 30-10, 13-38, 23-20 and 44-24 are left alone — both ends are pinned on a row and a col, so any move there would trade one alignment for another. 28, 18 and 37 take the first half of two-round walks (28 toward col 15 under 51; 18 toward row 7 to meet 2, with 37 kept one cell ahead of it so the col-26 V chain never swallows a point).

Round 4 — finish the two walks started in round 3 and start one more. 28 lands on col 15 under 51 (its 45-degree link becomes a real V, and 27-28 stays H because 28 never leaves row 52). 18 and 37 arrive on col 26 at rows 7 and 6, which puts 18 on row 7 with 2: 37 is deliberately kept one row ahead of 18 the whole way so the col-26 chain 37-18-20 never has an interior vertex sitting inside another segment. 16 starts a four-round walk east along its own locked row 41 toward col 35: the target is (35,41), which buys two alignments at once (16-58 becomes V on col 35 under 58, and 16-39 falls out as a one-cell 45-degree), so it is worth the walk even though no single round can cover 11 cells. The other seven off-segments (45-36, 36-23, 40-12, 30-10, 13-38, 38-18, 23-20) are now genuinely blocked: both endpoints of each are already pinned by an H and a V segment, so every candidate move there trades one alignment for another at best.

Round 5 — the remaining off-segments all have both endpoints pinned on a row and a col, so single-point moves cannot help; this round uses rigid group moves instead, where a whole locked chain shifts together and keeps every alignment it already had. (a) 30-10: instead of moving the pinned 10, I lift 30 one row to 35 and carry its leaf 41 with it, so 30-41 survives and 30-10 becomes H — row 35 is now the chain 58-24-10-30-41. (b) 40-12: the entire col-45 chain 40/10/9 slides three cols west onto col 42, which is 12's col. All three keep their own alignments (44-40 and 40-17 stay on row 31, 24-10 and 10-30 stay on row 35, 25-9 stays on row 42) and col 42 becomes the long trunk 38-12-40-10-9. (c) 45 and 20 start a three-round rigid descent to row 23, moving as a pair so 45-20 is H at every intermediate row; the payoff is 23-20 becoming H, which finishes a six-station trunk 45-20-23-12-22-46 across row 23. 0 walks down in lockstep five rows below 20 to keep its 45-degree link and to respect the quadrant rule, which forbids it crossing 20's row. (d) 16 continues east along row 41; note it must stop exactly on col 34 before reaching 35, because the quadrant rule will not let it jump from west of 39 to east of 39 in one move.
